description: In Athens, Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides invented tragedy. Chorus, hubris, catharsis: a theater built for thinking about the city.

hero.hook: Masks in the open sun, healing a city by shocking it.

blocks.text: In the 5th century BC, in Athens, **tragedy** was born. It was not private entertainment but a civic ritual, performed in front of thousands of citizens.
Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides invented an art that mixed gods, politics, and passion.
[[The chorus in Greek tragedy]] sang, danced, and commented on the action. The actors wore masks and played heroes and gods. A wealthy citizen paid for the show: this was the [[choregia]].
The Dionysia, the festivals of Dionysus, ran competitions. Tragedy was born inside that religious and civic frame. Winning honored the city as much as the god.

blocks.caption: The Theater of Epidaurus: acoustics as a miracle in stone

blocks.text: The tragic hero often gives in to [[hubris]], the excess that defies the order of things. The fall that follows is never gratuitous: it questions justice, fate, and responsibility.
Aeschylus added actors. Sophocles refined the psychology. Euripides unsettled every certainty. Three styles, one machine: make people think by moving them.
The [[deus ex machina]] sometimes lowered a god on a crane to untangle the plot, and audiences already complained that it was too convenient.
For Aristotle, tragedy produces [[catharsis]]: a cleansing through pity and terror. You leave shaken, but calmer. Theater treats the city by staging its fears.
The audience usually knew the myth already. The interest was not the twist, it was the handling. How would Oedipus fall? How would Antigone say no?

blocks.caption: Masks: emotion you can read from the back row

blocks.text: Shakespeare, opera, cinema: Greek tragedy is still the grammar of fate on stage. Our modern antiheroes owe it their downfalls.
To really grasp Greek tragedy and ancient theater, keep one thing in mind: every technical detail serves an emotion or an idea. The work is never merely decorative.
Context counts as much as style. Dates, places, patrons, audience: all of it explains why a form appears at one precise moment, and not before.
Finally, a legacy is measured over the long run. What we see today in museums, films, or popular music still carries the mark of these inventions.
From Wagnerian opera to disaster movies, the tragic structure survives. We have changed gods, not always falls.
In Athens, tragedy invented a civic theater where hubris, chorus, and catharsis taught a city to look at itself.
